items.title: Recapping the Yankees’ low-minors seasons
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
The minor-league season has officially come to an end, a season in which we saw a bit of a shift from the usual trend of Yankees’ minor league seasons.

We didn’t see too many midseason departures due to a weird deadline, we didn’t see a plethora of starting pitchers excel and we saw, for once, a group of hitting prospects that actually showed promise. Remember, entering this year, the No. 4 hitting prospect in the organization behind George Lombard Jr., Dax Kilby, and Spencer Jones was… who, exactly?

Scott will have you covered in the coming days with a Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders-intensive recap, but here’s the final evaluation of the rest of the full-season affiliates in a player-specific format, where I highlight some of the players to watch who defined the seasons at their respective levels.

Double

: The hitter with the best name brand here, Avina had a solid season all around in his first season in Double-A, but warts still remain. Acquired in the Jake Bauers trade after 2023 (who would’ve thought he’d turn into in Milwaukee), Avina was remarkably consistent all year through late July, even winning Eastern League Player of the Month after posting a 1.106 OPS in May.

However, as has been his bugaboo at times in his career, he ended the season in a slump, hitting just .229 with a 90 wRC+ in his final 41 games. It might’ve been the result of a midseason approach change, as he cut down on strikeouts at the expense of power production. When he was raking during the early summer, he was striking out nearly 30 percent of the time. He should get to Triple-A at some point next year, but I’m not convinced he’s passed all the tests to get there yet.

: Somerset’s MVP in 2026, the corner infielder was a 20/20 bat this year at the level, showing a side of him that we hadn’t quite seen. The 2023 18th-round pick out of Washington started his professional career with extremely little pop, but has slowly tapped into his raw power over the course of his career. Now finishing his age-24 season, Morales was reliable all season long in Somerset.

He finished slashing .282/.372/.479 with a 129 wRC+ while splitting time at first and third base. I’m not entirely sure of his big league projectability, but this is a guy who will be in Scranton next year. With 156 total games of Double-A experience, it’s time to see if he can sink or swim.

: There were a few quiet minor-league free agent signings who fared pretty well for the Yankees this year. Gladney is one of them, posting a 113 wRC+ in Double-A after spending six years in the White Sox organization. We’ll see if he re-ups on another minor league deal or heads elsewhere.

Every draft, the Yankees pick one guy who displayed big-time power in college and see if it translates. It doesn’t usually work, and it seemed like Moylan would be the latest example of the archetype failing in the pros… but maybe there’s something there. After struggling to hit much of anything through 2025, the 24-year-old finally got on a heater down in High-A before a late June promotion. After being called up, he posted a 118 wRC+ in 68 games in his first taste of Double-A. His 29 home runs were the most in the farm this year. Keep an eye on him.

Through late June, the closest catching prospect to the majors in the system was one of the worst hitters in the entire system, but he suddenly found something when the calendar flipped to August. After hitting one singular homer in his entire pro career through June 30th, he had six in July. In his final 150 plate appearances, he slashed .319/.351/.521. I’d have him repeat the level to see if those two months were a fluke or a sign of things to come.

Garrett Martin, Tyler Hardman, Marco Luciano: A grab bag of guys you’ll hear about from Scott in his Scranton roundup. These three guys were part of a historic start to the season for the Patriots, combining for 44 home runs in 550 plate appearances. Hardman hit a wall in Triple-A, the erstwhile Giants prospect Luciano did incredibly well and should push for a 40-man spot this offseason, and Martin suffered a season-ending injury in July. It’s a real shame; he was on pace to go well past 30/30 this season.

Just a really disappointing season from the former first-round pick. He had a 4.45 ERA in 56.2 innings, struggling with a high walk rate despite having stretches of brief brilliance with his enticing stuff. The injuries were rough, costing him a month early in the year and leaving him with a summer of building back up. Just a few weeks after finally getting back to full strength, he was put on the 60-day injured list. Next year will be big for him.

: This was Somerset’s best pitcher all season. In 81.1 innings, the former 16th-round pick pitched to a 3.65 ERA with a 22.0 K-BB%, boasting one of the largest strikeout rates of any Double-A pitcher by leaning heavily on his filthy secondaries. He hit a major wall in Triple-A and will have to fine-tune some things to avoid being the next Edgar Barclay with his low-90s fastball, but it was a step forward for a guy who has a case to be the org’s Minor League Pitcher of the Year.

If it’s not Rivas, it might be Fox. The Notre Dame product had a really strong debut season, tossing 130 total innings across two levels. What might be most impressive? After being so-so in Hudson Valley, he was aggressively pushed to Somerset in late July and excelled, pitching to a 3.97 ERA in eight starts across 47.2 innings. This guy eats innings like a bowl of cereal in the morning.

Not related to the Guardians’ closer, Smith had some prospect stock entering the season, but is likely off everyone’s boards after struggling to a 5.27 ERA in 124.2 innings. The 24-year-old former sixth-round pick will repeat the level in 2026 looking to find the stuff that had him jump up prospect lists in A-ball a few years ago.

A former Astros prospect acquired last July, Austin was Somerset’s closer in 2025, but had to repeat the level this year. I thought he might be able to break through into Scranton this year, but he battled some early struggles to make his season numbers more palatable towards the end, as the 25-year-old finished with a 3.61 ERA in 57 innings.

He earned a late-season promotion to Scranton for his exceptional work down here this season. When he was drafted, he sat 91-92. Now, two years after Tommy John surgery? How about 96-98? Command is still a bit of an issue, but he struck out 67 in 41.2 effective innings at this level this season.

The Yankees love to play with overage undrafted free agents with outlier traits in the bullpen. Rossi is quite old for a guy who made his pro debut last summer, but the 26-year-old has been exceptional at keeping the ball in the ballpark (3 HR allowed in 94 career innings) and racking up strikeouts. He had a 27.0 K-BB% in the minors this year while not allowing many homers and a .171 BAA. That’s not bad.

High-A Hudson Valley Renegades

It was a strong debut season for Jackson, who battled a few minor ailments (three different injured list stints) to have one of the more productive all-around seasons in the system, slashing .262/.360/.459 with 41 stolen bases in 101 games across two levels, being promoted in early August to Somerset. He spent much of the season at shortstop, but should settle at second or third base long term. The former fifth-round pick is in a good spot to be a featured face in Somerset in his age-23 season next year.

Remember me? The former uber-prospect revived his stock after a miserable two years in Tampa and a dreadful first two months in Hudson Valley, with an exceptional finish to the season, slashing .305/.377/.521 with a 133 wRC+ in his final 83 games across two levels. He’s still extremely athletically gifted and just turned 22 years old. He popped some big exit velocities and displayed tremendous arm strength, splitting time at shortstop and third base this year. He has a toolkit; let’s keep an eye on him next year.

Is this the new best catching prospect in the system? Hard to say. Genther, a former outfielder from Rhode Island, converted to catcher after signing as an undrafted free agent last summer and spent this season as a work in progress on both sides. He bounced back from a putrid start (0 HR in first 40 games) to ultimately finish as the Renegades’ best hitter, and should get to go to Somerset next year. Now, he is an extreme work in progress behind the plate, allowing a truly baffling number of stolen bases (196 in 65 starts).

You don’t hear of many players coming from Puerto Rico anymore because of how their pipeline has changed over the years, but Rodriguez is the organization’s most notable Puerto Rican as a former 17th-round pick. He was a pretty niche prospect for his entire career, but got hot in June (.319/.396/.615) to put himself on the map. He unfortunately suffered a season-ending injury in late July, but having just turned 22, there’s time for him to become someone.

: Another former undrafted free agent, McCann split time across three different levels this year, but never stopped displaying his raw power. The 22-year-old from Virginia Tech slugged .544 in the first 68 games of his pro career and also saw time at first base this season.

He’s a fun prospect. A six-game cameo in Tampa last year got a lot of people excited about the Missouri alum’s potential, but the former 16th-round pick looked like one for much of the season, with big contact issues delaying a seemingly overdue promotion to this level. After he got to Hudson Valley? He stepped up his game, reining in those whiff issues and rediscovering his unique power-speed combo. He finished with 24 home runs and 41 stolen bases, the first Yankee to reach those numbers in 32 years.

For much of this season, a guy who’s been hyped as one of the organization’s best pitching prospects looked pretty tough. He was able to routinely go deep into games, but he struggled with command and missing bats, posting a single-digit K-BB% all season long. Due to the roster churn and promotions, he got a late promotion to Somerset and actually finished really strong, posting three consecutive starts of at least six innings with 21 total strikeouts to zero walks. It was also nice to see him build up to 105 innings after his injuries last year.

The stuff is absolutely there for Facundo to be in the big leagues one day; it’s just not going to be as a starter. The Yankees finally got him out of Tampa in April and he showed he can stay healthy, but he wasn’t able to show he can consistently throw strikes. The 24-year-old walked 71 batters in 99 innings in Hudson Valley, but also struck out 123. He should probably be put in the bullpen next year and sent to Somerset to expedite his high-level stuff.

Entering this season, you could lump Serna in a group with Henry Lalane as damaged goods after years of injuries, but the 22-year-old found an unlikely revival in 2026, just by finally being able to stay healthy. He blew past his prior career high of 69.1 innings to toss 118.2 and set the Hudson Valley single-season strikeout record at 140, while reasonably managing his walks. The ERA was still pretty average at 4.32 in 23 starts, but he’s back on the prospect radar after vanishing following a brilliant 2021 and 2022.

45.1 IP, 3.18 ERA, 3.18 FIP, 1.28 WHIP, 16.3 K-BB%41.2 IP, 3.67 ERA, 4.44 FIP, 1.49 WHIP, 10.5 K-BB%44 IP, 3.48 ERA, 3.78 FIP, 1.32 WHIP, 19.0 K-BB% 51 IP, 2.82 ERA, 3.84 FIP, 1.24 WHIP, 16.1 K-BB%35 IP, 3.86 ERA, 4.36 FIP, 1.14 WHIP, 25.4 K-BB%

: It was a lost season for Kilby, who missed several months due to recurring hamstring issues. This was a guy who had skyrocketed into the Top 100 lists entering the season, but only managed 154 plate appearances due to an exceptionally low start. The only two things I really got out of his season? He’s absolutely not a shortstop down the road (second base, third base, or center field seem more likely), and he has one of the best eyes of any 19-year-old I’ve ever seen. He had a 25.3-percent walk rate this season. The Arizona Fall League awaits.

: I will try to not be a prisoner of the moment, but this might be the best prospect in the system. A 6-foot-4 athletic freak from the D.R., Pena is just 18 years old and hit historically well in the DSL, becoming the first Yankee in nine years to skip the GCL/FCL and go straight to full-season ball, where he barely slowed down. He finished the season hitting over .350 with truly alien exit velocities for a player his age, strong defense in center field (with a cannon for an arm), and plus-plus speed. This is the most tool-heavy guy in the entire system and I am super excited about 2027 for him.

: Who had the best overall numbers for this elite Tampa offense? It was actually Luis Escudero, who slashed .288/.455/.556 in 202 plate appearances after spending the spring at the complex. The 20-year-old packs a lot of pop in a small, 5-foot-8 frame, and somehow managed to have an even better eye than Kilby this year. There wasn’t enough sample to have him go to High-A to start next season, but he’ll be there soon if he continues to produce.

: Do you miss Jesus Rodriguez in the system? Here’s your new favorite prospect. Puello is basically a baby Rodriguez, already having experience at catcher, first base, left field, and right field. I’m not sure what his long-term position is, but if any organization can get this guy catching in order, it’s this one. His bat also looks great, smacking 14 home runs in 73 games with some solid game power.

: In the most recent edition of “former multi-million prospect shows life,” Mayea looked really bad to start the season, but found something over the course of the regular season. I’m going to need to see a lot more to be truly convinced the 20-year-old is on the right path, but he hit .298 across his final 47 games. Now if he could only find the power…

Way too little sample for much on any of these guys. Here’s a sampler:

  • Tyce Armstrong, the guy who once hit three grand slams in a game, carried that Big 12 power into Single-A, finishing the season on an absolute heater.
  • Anthony Potestio, the 11th-round pick, is getting a lot of buzz for how well he handled Single-A pitching as someone who didn’t play in the SEC or Big 12. In 19 games, he slashed .333/.513/.684.
  • Paul Gutierrez-Contreras II has been the most impressive in terms of exit velocities. He’s pumped out a handful of batted balls over 105 mph already.

A 2025 undrafted free agent, Boudreau came out of nowhere to be one of the most productive starting pitchers in the system. In 103 innings, he posted a 3.41 ERA with a 17.3 K-BB% and even struck out six in 3.1 shutout innings in a brief Somerset cameo. This is a guy who will have an opportunity to get himself on the map in Hudson Valley next year.

Mr. Consistency. West started the season with some growing pains, but ended it as the most effective starter in the system. The 22-year-old finished the season by pitching to a 2.23 ERA across his final 10 starts, averaging six full innings per start. He just got better and better over the course of the season.

Oh boy. Mac Heuer suffered a season-ending injury in July. Thatcher Hurd started the season recovering from Tommy John surgery, made eight solid starts, and finished the year injured. Brennan Stuprich spent several months on the injured list. J.T. Etheridge was also only limited to 13 starts, but he finished the season extremely strong and will be a sneaky pitcher to watch in the AFL next month.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Bobby Shantz
items.author: Nick Power
items.content:
“But it turned out awful nice, I’ll tell you that — 16 years. You know, I lasted more than I thought I would. Boy, what a life. I really enjoyed every minute of it. Even when I was horseshit, I still liked it.”

As he approached his 100th birthday in 2025, Bobby Shantz took the opportunity to reflect on his career in baseball. More than 60 years since he’d hung up his cleats, he still had the mind of a ballplayer, reminiscing about the legends he played with and against with vividness and vibrancy. But he also had the perspective of a man who’d been on a long journey — and was grateful for every stop along the way.

September 26, 1925 (Pottstown, PA)1957-60

Shantz grew up in the suburbs in Pennsylvania. A small kid (his height peaked at 5-foot-6 as an adult), the young Bobby distinguished himself through pinpoint control and all-around athleticism. After his high school coach refused to let him pitch due to his size, a youth baseball manager saw Shantz working out his curveball and decided to give him a shot on the mound. He joined the Army in 1944 and continued to hone his craft on Army baseball teams while stationed in the Philippines, competing against big-leaguers and building confidence in his ability to go pro.

Upon his return to the States, Shantz continued to impress in semipro ball but struggled to find any takers among MLB teams due to his stature. Finally, after a couple of teammates with connections in the Philadelphia A’s organization put in a good word, Harry O’Donnell, a scout with the team, signed him to an A-Ball deal. He immediately impressed, winning 18 games in 28 starts and striking out nearly a batter an inning. The next year, at the age of 23, he made the leap all the way to the big leagues, where he would be managed by none other than Hall of Famer and baseball lifer Connie Mack.

In his first three seasons in Philly, the southpaw established himself as a strong contributor, pitching around league average and making his first All-Star team in 1951. But it was the following year that would be Shantz’s campaign for the ages. Seemingly out of nowhere, he emerged as the best pitcher in baseball, winning 24 games, posting a 152:63 K:BB ratio, recording a 2.48 ERA, 9.4 rWAR, and taking home the AL MVP. The career year was aided in part by the use of a knuckleball Mack had forbade him from employing but his new manager, Jimmie Dykes, encouraged.

In the ‘52 All-Star Game, Shantz struck out the side in his only inning of work, including punchouts of Jackie Robinson and Stan Musial. His newfound stardom even netted him a guest spot on the Ed Sullivan Show.

As is so often the case after a superlative season like Shantz’s ‘52, the pitcher took a step back in the years that followed. As he struggled with injury and inconsistency, he went 13-26 with a 4.42 ERA over the next four years, failing to recapture his peak form on floundering A’s teams as the franchise moved to Kansas City. After the ‘56 campaign, the A’s traded their former MVP to the Yankees as part of a 13-player trade. Shantz was a man reborn, leading all of baseball with a 2.45 ERA in ‘57 and earning his first All-Star berth since his MVP season.

Shantz also took home the very first AL Gold Glove for a pitcher, his first of eight such awards earned between both leagues. The man’s legacy as one of the greatest fielding pitchers has never been in question. “I’ll occasionally hear a guy introduce me and say, ‘He was the best fielding pitcher in baseball,’ and I’ll say, ‘No, Bobby Shantz was,’” said Jim Kaat, winner of 16 Gold Gloves himself. “He didn’t win a Gold Glove until ’57. Had they given them out starting in ’50, he would have had 16 or 17 as well.”

Shantz made the only World Series start of his long career that October, taking the ball in Game 2 against the Milwaukee Braves. He struggled, allowing four runs (three earned) in three innings, but rebounded well in Game 4, tossing three scoreless innings in relief to keep the Yankees in a game they’d eventually tie up in the ninth.

Shantz spent three more years in pinstripes, eventually transitioning to a bullpen role, where he pitched well as a proto-closer. Despite finding his greatest individual success in Philadelphia, Shantz would later recount that his time with the Yankees—who won a championship in 1958 and the pennant in three of his four seasons there—was the most rewarding of his career.

After the ‘60 season, the Yankees left him exposed in an expansion draft. Shantz was selected by the Washington Senators, who flipped him to the Pirates. He’d spend the final four seasons of his career in a state of perpetual motion, pitching for five different teams as a trusted reliever. After the ‘64 season, at the age of 39, Shantz retired. The 5-foot-6 non-prospect who was rejected repeatedly at the start of his career had stuck around for 16 years in the big leagues.

Shantz retired back to Pennsylvania, where he managed a restaurant and co-owned a bowling alley. In 2010, Pottstown High School renamed their baseball park Bobby Shantz Field in honor of their famous alumnus.

As the years have gone on and he’s passed the century mark, Shantz has increasingly become the “oldest living” designee in many areas — oldest living MLB MVP, oldest living A’s player, and on down the line. He’s accepted this status with grace and humor, giving colorful interviews and staying connected to the game he loves.

On the occasion of his 101st birthday, we celebrate the oldest living Yankee, Bobby Shantz. We’ll let him take us out in his own words: “I had a great life. Jesus, great life. Boy, I’d like to do that all over again.”

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Yankees Rivalry Roundup: AL West madness reaches new low
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
Having moved a scheduled Saturday game against the Orioles up to Friday for a straight doubleheader, the Yankees and O’s split the twin bill. Baltimore blew out Brendan Beck and company in a 10-2 loss in the opener—an ignominious follow-up to CC Sabathia’s number retirement—but Ryan Yarbrough and Will Warren combined to lead them to 17 strikeouts in the 6-3 nightcap win. Most importantly, everyone remained healthy. Wins and losses don’t matter for the regular season at this point! Now, they wait at home for the storm to pass today and see if they can play a Game 162 tomorrow. If not … see you on Tuesday for the Wild Card Series, Boston.

Here’s what else was going on Friday among the remaining AL playoff hopefuls.

Tampa Bay Rays (97-63) 2, Philadelphia Phillies (87-73) 0

We’ll only take a minute on this one since—with all due respect to the playoff hopes of our friends in Philly (but boy is it suddenly getting tense with the Diamondbacks hot on the trail)—it really doesn’t mean much with Tampa Bay locked into the top AL seed. The Phils got a really nice outing from ace Cristopher Sánchez, who fanned 10 Rays in seven innings of work. But he did allow an RBI single to Jonny DeLuca in the first and a solo shot to catcher Nick Fortes in the second, and with the Phillies absolutely sputtering … yeah, that was it. Freddy Peralta blanked Philly through 5.1 before a quartet of relievers completed the four-hit shutout, Bryan Baker notching his 41st save of the season.

Boston Red Sox (86-74) 4, Chicago Cubs (88-72) 3 [Game 1]

It took a little longer than anyone expected, but the Red Sox officially locked themselves into the No. 5 seed in the American League and a date with the Yankees in the Wild Card Series. The best-of-three will begin on Tuesday with all games in the Bronx. At first, it seemed like Boston’s odd skid would continue when the Cubbies plated three within the first four outs. Tyrone Taylor had doubled in Seiya Suzuki following a one-out walk in the first, and the trio of Matt Shaw, Michael Busch, and No. 9 hitter Miguel Amaya continued the mini-parade against Alec Gamboa in the second with with a single and a pair of doubles, Amaya’s going off the Green Monster to drive in a pair.

Part of that rally had involved Shaw getting thrown out on a grounder to third though, and Chicago never scored that fourth run. They would rue that result, with typical starter Jake Bennett getting his first relief appearance in anticipation of the Wild Card showdown and throwing 3.2 scoreless. Greg Weissert and Raymond Burgos continued to keep the Cubs off the board for the rest of the game as their offense rallied off Clay Holmes. A rare error by Dansby Swanson brought in the first Boston run in the fourth, and Holmes allowed a leadoff single to former Yankees teammate Isiah Kiner-Falefa in the fifth, followed by a Roman Anthony double. He got one more out, but Caleb Thielbar entered and allowed a game-tying knock from Adley Rutschman.

The Red Sox took the lead in the seventh, breaking the tie off Aaron Civale when Anthony tripled and Connor Wong doubled him in. With Weissert and Burgos silencing Chicago, that was all she wrote. The only downside for Boston was that surprise story Mickey Gasper had to leave the game early with biceps discomfort.

Boston Red Sox (87-74) 2, Chicago Cubs (88-73) 0 [Game 2]

The weather got gloomier as the day went along but the Red Sox left Fenway with a clean doubleheader sweep. Boston kept Brayan Bello in playoff tune-up mode despite coming off an outing of eight innings of 11-K, one-run ball, and they still twirled a shutout. Bello blanked Chicago through four, departed with his pitch count at 58, and gave way to rookie Jedixson Paez, making his fifth career appearance. Paez outpitched Bello, fanning five in five shutout frames to earn his first career win.

David Peterson’s own five zeroes for the Cubs were in vain. The scoreless tie was broken up in the eighth with IKF and Jahmai Jones (another former Yankee) on base after walks. Wilyer Abreu cracked a double off Ryan Rolison to plate both runners. That was all Boston needed. The Cubs had hoped to host a Wild Card Series at Wrigley, but that’s looking unlikely now with the Padres a game and a half ahead of them. Game 162 will determine their flight path, and they’ll need a flight just to play it. The nor’easter is not supposed to get any better in Beantown over the weekend, so the Sunday game will be at a neutral site: Tropicana Field. Let’s get weird.

Texas Rangers (79-81) 2, Minnesota Twins (76-84) 10

When Jacob deGrom was rehabbing from Tommy John surgery, opportunities like this one undoubtedly drove him. Yes, the AL West is lousy, but the Rangers can easily win it and they had deGrom out there against a team playing out the string in the Twins. Even with Joe Ryan on the bump opposing him, they felt great. Instead, Minnesota clobbered deGrom and tallied six in the second, Luke Keaschall delivering the big blow on a two-run triple. The two-time Cy Young Award winner was tagged for eight runs in four innings of work. The news got worse for the Rangers learned that top bat Josh Jung broke his hand on a hit-by-pitch; he’s likely done for 2026. This one had to hurt, and deGrom was furious at himself in the postgame, saying multiple times that he was “embarrassed.”

Houston Astros (79-81) 5, The Athletics (64-96) 6

Well don’t worry Jacob because remember: the AL West is lousy. The Rangers lost while the Astros were still playing on Friday, so they had a golden opportunity to seize control of the AL West, especially because they own the tiebreaker and were facing a terrible A’s team. Said terrible A’s team held off Houston and won, 6-5. A six-run sixth proved to be enough for the A’s offense as Hunter Brown’s once-solid outing went by the wayside with awful relief from Bennett Sousa, who failed to record a single out and allowed three runs. Henry Bolte smacked a two-run triple in the frame and the A’s had a commanding 6-1 lead.

Houston did fight back, in part because the A’s bullpen is horrific. Cam Smith homered and a rally in the eighth broke the score to 6-5 with runners on second and third after a wild pitch. Baby Bomber alum Luis Medina fanned Smith though and Houston was held at bay. Nelson Velázquez got a one-out walk in the ninth to put the go-ahead run on against Hogan Harris, only to be erased on a Jeremy Peña double play ball, stranding Yordan Alvarez in the on-deck circle. For the first time in MLB history, we are guaranteed a full-season division winner with either a .500 record or worse because neither Houston nor Texas can be better than 81-81.

Cleveland Guardians (84-76) 12, Kansas City Royals (68-92) 9

Funky one in KC. The Guardians maintained their hot streak and withstood rallies from the Royals to win late without actually getting all that many hits. They had a dozen runs scored but only nine hits. Carter Jensen slugged two homers and drove in five for the Royals, but it wasn’t nearly enough, even with a tied-up ballgame at 7-7. walks and a fielder’s choice in the eighth led to Cleveland plating three without a hit before the surging Angel Martinez drove in two with a double to make it a 12-7 game. Salvador Perez’s 324th career homer cut into the lead in the ninth, but the Guardians held on to maintain their one-game lead in the AL Central.

Chicago White Sox (83-77) 6, Colorado Rockies (57-103) 1

Munetaka Murakami clobbered a pair of dingers to reach 35 in his rookie MLB season, and both came off countryman Tomoyuki Sugano, who he’d homered against twice in NPB play. Sean Burke threw 5.1 innings with one run allowed, and all that was easily plenty for the Pale Hose to take care of business on the South Side. They’ll just need some help from KC if they’re going to pass Cleveland for the division again.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 9/26/26
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
A good chunk of the East Coast is getting slammed by a nor’easter this weekend, so if you’re in the area, we hope you stay safe! Since this current Yankees series against the Orioles is meaningless aside from the obvious goal of staying healthy, the game originally scheduled for today was played yesterday in a straight doubleheader. They’ll take a beat today and try to play tomorrow (rookie Elmer Rodríguez is announced as the probable starter for New York in a cameo), but if it doesn’t work out, it doesn’t work out. We may just have a 161-game regular season.

Anyway, the postseason looms on Tuesday! Monday’s league-wide offday is the calm before the storm, but we’ll have plenty of material coming up then so consider today our personal Pinstripe Alley calm before the storm. It’s not all quiet though, as I’m on the Rivalry Roundup, Nick is celebrating the 101st (!) birthday of the oldest living Yankee, and Michael is discussing how the Yankees’ low-minors teams fared in 2026.

Game preemptively moved up to yesterday for a twin bill, so it’s an offday with Game 162 tomorrow

1. Assuming Carlos Rodón is not in the Wild Card Series rotation, what do you think is the best spot to potentially deploy him out of the bullpen?

2. Think the Phillies continue their collapse and let the Diamondbacks steal the last NL Wild Card spot from them?

items.title: Yankees news: Schlittler, Fried still both in play to start Game 1
items.author: Jake Devin
items.content:
MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: Cam Schlittler put the finishing touches on his Cy Young season Thursday night against the Rays. It wasn’t his sharpest start, Schlittler needing 70 pitches to navigate three innings, but it put his ERA on the season at 1.95, the lowest mark by a Yankee starter since Ron Guidry posted a 1.74 ERA in his legendary 1978 season, and the third-lowest ERA in franchise history. It’s also the lowest ERA by an American League starer since Justin Verlander’s 1.75 ERA in 2022, which won the future Hall of Famer* his third Cy Young.

*Incidentally, Verlander is making his final career start today in Detroit.

New York Post | Dan Martin: Speaking of Schlittler, you’d expect a pitcher of his stature to be a shoe-in for Game 1 of a playoff series. However, the Yankees are considering saving him for Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series. Max Fried could start Game 1, on extra rest, and thus also give Schlittler an extra day of rest before the Yankees embark on what they hope will be a long postseason run. Schlittler would have enough rest to start Games 2 and 5 of a potential ALDS regardless of whether he pitches Game 1 or 2 of the Wild Card Series. Is it possible the Yankees are overthinking it? Yes, admits pitching coach Matt Blake, but these are precisely the things the club’s staff is paid to overthink.

Whichever way the Yankees line things up, the good news is that their excellent rotation means that they’ll have an ace-caliber talent going every night. As an aside, Andrés wrote up this debate for earlier in the week, and that’s worth a read if you haven’t checked it out yet.

The Athletic | Evan Drellich and Andrew Marchand: Drellich and Marchand report on the looming lockout, and one mark to look out for next year: 60 games. Apparently, if MLB misses 60 or more games in the 2027 season, the league’s national broadcast contracts would extend an extra year, into 2029. That introduces an interesting wrinkle into the owners’ calculus when it comes to this round of labor negotiations. On the one hand, the league would still receive their negotiated dues as part of their deals with their broadcast partners. On the other, extending those deals another year means the league can’t negotiate new national deals for another year; the league is likely seeking to earn a hefty raise on their next round of national contracts. The league also wouldn’t get paid in 2029 under this scenario. 

SNY | John Flanigan: Ryan Weathers threw a live bullpen session yesterday, facing hitters including Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham. Aaron Boone said Weathers was up to 96 mph on his fastball, though called his control a little “scattered.” According to Boone, Weathers is on track to be an option during the playoffs, but it’s unclear if the Yankees will put the left-hander on the Wild Card roster. Carlos Lagrange also threw to hitters at Yankee Stadium yesterday, though it’s unlikely he’ll be on the playoff roster soon. Boone said he isn’t in play for the Wild Card roster and Matt Blake threw cold water on the idea of him debuting in the playoffs, though it still remains a (remote) possibility that Lagrange could factor into the Yankees’ plans later in the postseason if the team advances and Lagrange’s rehab continues to go well.

items.title: Yankees pitchers strike out a whopping 17 to split Orioles doubleheader
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
It wasn’t exactly a meaningful game, but the Yankees projected a much better image in the nightcap against the Baltimore Orioles and won it 6-3 after losing the first game in ugly fashion. New York’s pitchers certainly brought the strikeout stuff for this one, as Ryan Yarbrough, Will Warren, Brent Headrick, John Schreiber, and Alexander Cornielle combined to punch out 17 — tied for a team sign high among standard nine-inning efforts with a gem led by Cam Schlittler’s 13 on June 19th against the Reds.

The Yankees’ record is now 93-68 with one regular season game left. If the weather holds off (no guarantees there), they have a shot at matching last year’s 94-68 record, which is frankly not bad because their best player, Aaron Judge, only suited up for 66 games.

This game actually started as a pitchers’ duel, with Orioles’ starter Brandon Young and Yarbrough trading zeroes for the first 2.1 innings. The lefty departed after 49 pitches, but did not allow a run despite surrendering four hits and a walk, fanning five.

The Yankees brought in Warren with one out and a runner on first, which represented a nice training scenario ahead of his expected bullpen role in the Wild Card Series.

As it turned out, Warren was amazing, even though he allowed a double in that same inning that could have produced a run for Baltimore, and covered 3.2 scoreless frames while conceding a mere three hits and racking up seven strikeouts. He will finish the regular season with a nice 3.92 ERA and just over a strikeout per inning.

The Yankees finally got to Young in the bottom of the fifth. After two outs, Austin Wells walked and crossed home thanks to Ryan McMahon’s RBI double.

Young pitched a very solid game, completing five frames in which he conceded a single run on two hits and three walks. He whiffed six and finished the game and the season with a 3.56 ERA.

The Bombers extended their lead in the bottom of the sixth against the O’s bullpen. Spencer Jones singled in Heliot Ramos, aided by a fielding error by right fielder Rece Hinds. Later in the inning, Anthony Volpe (playing shortstop with George Lombard Jr. getting a rare rest) hit an automatic double that plated Luis García Jr. and Jones to make it a 4-0 ballgame.

Headrick replaced Warren in the seventh and surrendered the Orioles’ first run. With the bases loaded and one out, Leody Taveras hit a sac fly to bring in Pete Alonso. Ramos and García would hit consecutive RBI singles in the bottom of the inning, though, and the Yankees were up 6-1.

Cornielle entered for his MLB debut, and was promptly greeted by a Dylan Beavers homer to right, making it a 6-2 ballgame. The rookie got into some trouble after the long ball, putting two men on base before getting the first out. He then surrendered a very long RBI double to Taveras that just missed the stands, as the O’s trimmed the Yankees lead to three runs.

Cornielle then shook it off and struck out the next two hitters to end the ballgame on a high note. Ben Rice went 2-for-3 with a double, a walk, and a run scored, and McMahon went 2-for-4 with a double, a run, and an RBI. Volpe plated two, and Wells walked twice and scored once.

The Yankees are supposed to wrap up their season on Sunday against the Orioles, starting at 3:20pm ET. Elmer Rodríguez has been announced as New York’s starter. However, the nor’easter that forced this doubleheader in the first place has led to some bad forecasts for Sunday, so it’s very possible that Game 162 gets nixed. We’ll find out soon enough! Stay dry out there.

items.title: New York Yankees vs. Baltimore Orioles: Ryan Yarbrough vs. Brandon Young
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
After CC Sabathia’s No. 52 retirement ceremony and a rather forgettable Game 1 of Friday’s doubleheader, the New York Yankees will take the field again and face the Baltimore Orioles in the nightcap. The Bombers already know that they will host the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round, and the O’s are already eliminated from playoff contention.

As a result, this is merely a tune-up game for New York, but that’s certainly not insignificant ahead of another edition of their rivalry with the Sox. Brandon Young will take the ball for Baltimore, trying to wrap up a solid year. The 28-year-old followed up his mediocre 57.2-inning cameo last year with a very solid campaign in 2026, with 151.2 frames of a 3.62 ERA, a 4.53 FIP, and 127 punchouts. He is not a star, but did more than enough to win a long-term spot on the O’s staff.

The Yankees, with that series against their bitter rivals looming, didn’t announce their starting pitcher for Game 2 of the doubleheader until just about 10 minutes ago. Long reliever Ryan Yarbrough gets the nod for his second start of the season; he last pitched on Tuesday. His only other start of 2026 was the second game of another doubleheader against the Dodgers, when he went 2.2 shutout innings back on July 19th.

Yarbrough is obviously not built up length-wise to go deep in this one either, but the expectation is that Will Warren will pitch a couple innings as preparation for the playoffs. He last pitched on Sunday in Arizona. Big things were expected from Warren this season, and while he didn’t exactly develop into an ace, he has been steady as a rock with a 4.02 ERA in 152.1 innings. A team would take that from its No. 5 starter any day of the week. David Bednar, Brent Headrick, and Paul Blackburn can only pitch so much, so Warren could certainly make a positive impact in the ‘pen.

Also keep an eye on the bullpen for Alexander Cornielle. A career minor-league signed before the season, the right-hander made 16 starts for Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre and was activated to the big-league roster between games with matinee starter Brendan Beck optioned. If he appears tonight or Sunday, it will be his MLB debut.

From this point forward, everything the Yankees do on the field will be with the Red Sox in mind, so don’t expect an all-out effort from those expected to be on the Wild Card Series roster. Indeed, there isn’t a ton of overlap between the Game 1 lineup and the Game 2 starting nine, as the Yankees are avoiding using too many players if possible. Indeed, the Game 1 infield went Paul Goldschmidt/José Caballero/George Lombard Jr./Anthony Volpe from first to third, and Game 2 has Luis García Jr./Jazz Chisholm Jr./Volpe/Ryan McMahon, with Volpe giving Lombard a spell by shifting over to his familiar six for the first time since his early-August demotion. Cody Bellinger tags in for Heliot Ramos in left, while Ramos shifts to right and Amed Rosario takes a seat. Austin Wells will catch and Spencer Jones is the only one starting the same position in both games, in center.

: Yankee Stadium – Bronx, NY

: 7:30 p.m. ET

: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280

Gotham Sports App, MLB.tv (out-of-market only)

items.title: Yankees flop after CC Sabathia ceremony, lose to Orioles
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
With nothing left to play for on either side, the Yankees vs. Orioles series opener was somewhat overshadowed with the number retirement ceremony for CC Sabathia that took place before the game. The expected bad weather tomorrow forced a doubleheader today and moved the ceremony up to this afternoon as well. The short notice change led to the stands being emptier than anyone would like, but it was still a nice ceremony for the now-forever Yankees’ No. 52. Old friends Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, Dellin Betances, and Chris Young joined in the festivities on the field, alongside Sabathia’s family.

On the field, things could’ve gone better.

Making something of a spot start with the doubleheader and the Yankees planning ahead for the postseason, Brendan Beck started for the Yankees. Not that it was something the Yankees were considering, but Beck didn’t particularly make a case to be a last-second playoff roster addition. In his five innings, he allowed seven runs on six hits and three walks, including two home runs. The bullpen wasn’t particularly lights out following him, allowing the Orioles to build up a big lead.

The Yankees’ offense was always going to be up against it considering that fact, but they didn’t do much. Orioles starter Trevor Rogers mostly kept the Yankees in check as Baltimore kept adding on. The Yankees could only plate one run from their eight hits, dooming them to a 10-2 loss in the first game of the doubleheader.

On the mound, Beck started things off with a couple scoreless innings. However, Baltimore got on the board in the third. Beck nearly got through the inning again, but issued a two-out walk to Dylan Beavers. That came back to haunt him, as Pete Alonso did a Pete Alonso thing and homered to put the O’s in front.

An inning later, Beck loaded the bases after walking two and allowing a single. Christian Franklin then dropped in a single, plating another Orioles’ run. After a force out got a runner at home, Beavers took Beck deep for a grand slam, putting Baltimore well in front.

The Yankees got on the board themselves in the bottom of the fourth. Heliot Ramos reached with a triple, aided by center fielder Colton Cowser misplaying the carom off the wall. Amed Rosario followed that with an easy single to score the Yankees’ first run.

Baltimore got that run back a short time later, thanks to an outfield miscue of the Yankees’ own. With reliever Yerry De los Santos in for the Yankees, Jeremiah Jackson hit a ball to deep right-center. The ball just got over the glove of Spencer Jones and took a fortuitous bounce past him. Jackson managed to race all the way around and beat the throw home for an inside-the-park homer, the first one in the Bronx in a dozen years — coincidentally with today’s honoree on the mound against Wil Myers. Alonso added a more conventional homer in the seventh in that it went over the fence, but it was unconventional in that it was an absolute bomb, 471 feet away.

Honestly, I can’t even be mad at that one. Baltimore would tack on one more run to get to double digits for the game. Paul Blackburn and David Bednar got their work in as expected, and we now won’t see them again until the Wild Card Series.

The Yankees did get one run back after Spencer Jones singled in the bottom of the ninth and eventually came around to score on a Paul Goldschmidt sacrifice fly. Ben Rice struck out looking to end it.

One pretty disappointing thing to come out of the game was the play of the offense. Yes, the game didn’t actually mean anything, but the Yankees did send out the likes of Goldschmidt and Rosario and their theoretical “lefty” lineup. Them not doing much on offense isn’t what you would want to see considering that the Red Sox Wild Card Series lineup is now locked in and Boston has a bunch of left-handed pitchers they can throw at the Yankees.

The second game of today’s doubleheader is set to begin at 7:30pm ET, which New York just announced. Brandon Young will go for Baltimore, while the Yankees will counter with Ryan Yarbrough, with Will Warren expected to provide relief work in anticipation of his playoff role.

items.title: How to watch Yankees vs. Red Sox in AL Wild Card Series: Start times, channels, and more
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The MLB postseason is finally upon us, and the No. 4 seed Yankees are kicking things off by facing the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, just as they did in 2025. New York will end the season at least four games better than Boston, but as they say, all records reset to 0-0 come October — or very-late September in the case of the 2026 season.

The Red Sox defeated the Cubs on Friday afternoon to officially clinch the No. 5 seed, meaning the Yankees will have home-field advantage by starting the postseason in the Bronx. They already knew they would be hosting, but it wasn’t yet official that they would face Boston. Per MLB’s Sarah Langs, this will be the seventh all-time postseason meeting between the Yanks and Red Sox, tied for the second-most common matchup in league history and trailing only the 12 famous Yankees/Dodgers World Series rumbles. New York and Boston have each won three series apiece in the playoff head-to-heads.

You won’t want to miss all the action in the best-of-three series next week, with the winner advancing to face the Rays in the American League Division Series in a race for the pennant.

Here’s all the information you’ll need to know to tune into every game this weekend. This post will be updated with first pitch times as soon as they are announced, though given the hubbub that usually surrounds Yankees/Red Sox, it would be a surprise if they weren’t all night games.

How to watch Yankees vs. Red Sox in Wild Card Series

items.title: New York Yankees vs. Baltimore Orioles: Brendan Beck vs. Trevor Rogers
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
Expected inclement weather of Saturday led to the Yankees and Orioles moving around their weekend regular season finale and playing two games today on Friday. Today’s opener will feature the CC Sabathia number retirement ceremony that was originally set for tomorrow. After that pomp and circumstance, the Yankees and O’s will get their three game set going.

In the first of today’s games, the Yankees will give the start to Brendan Beck, who was just called up alongside Yerry De los Santos with Luis Gil and Bradley Hanner farmed out last night. So far, Beck has made three MLB appearances since debuting earlier this season. He has an 8.22 ERA in 7.2 innings, including five runs allowed in 3.2 innings back on July 4th, which was his first career MLB start. Between the playoffs coming up and today now being a doubleheader, the Yankees more than anything will be hoping he can soak up some innings.

Backing up him, the Yankees will be running out their lefty lineup, sending out Paul Goldschmidt and Amed Rosario. Ali Sánchez will be behind the plate before switching with Austin Wells for the nightcap.

With the lefty lineup starting, the Yankees will be facing, as you might guess, a lefty. Trevor Rogers will be going for Baltimore. He has a 4.07 ERA in 165.2 innings this season. This could be his last start with the Orioles after a very up-and-down tenure that began at the 2024 Trade Deadline, as he is a free agent at season’s end.

We hope that you’ll come join us in the game thread for all of today’s action, so here’s how to watch the opener today.

: 4:05 p.m. ET
